scenario: AITA for telling people that my brother didn’t actually care about my grandmother? | My grandmother passed away, and we just buried her yesterday. She was 89. She was pretty independent up until a fall that made her less mobile. My aunt took care of her in the final year. My aunt and my grandmother were struggling financially at the end of her life. I would say my brother and I are both financially stable. I would often float them money to get food, medication, etc. But when they called him, they got radio silence. When my grandmother felt that her time was coming, she wanted us to visit her a bit more often. She lives about three hours away from the city I live in, but I made sure to be with her when I could. My brother lives two hours away, and didn’t see her for the entire year. When I saw her she would ask me if he was mad at her, and why he didn’t call. So it was a surprise to me when he began acting hysterical at her funeral. He was crying, he was screaming. He held onto her hand and sobbed when they opened the casket. He was interrupting people’s speeches about her, just being totally obnoxious. He even tried to throw himself on the casket when they were lowering it into the ground. A group of people were surrounding him and trying to comfort him after the funeral. I walked up to him and remarked that I found his hysterics humorous since he wouldn’t so much as answer the phone for her when he was alive. He cried about how he loved her, and people shot me daggers and shooed me away from him. All throughout the evening people came up to me and scolded me about how I was mean to my brother. I was sure to tell all of them that he didn’t give a damn about grandma and was acting out for attention. People gave me the cold shoulder for the rest of the evening. They told me to have compassion because I am the older sibling. I think he’s an asshole and being an attention whore. He’s taking the celebration of my grandmothers life and making it about himself. Who is the asshole here?

Jewish tradition emphasizes *derekh eretz* (basic courtesy and compassion), *shmirat halashon* (guarding one's tongue), and * nichum aveilim* (comforting the bereaved). A funeral is a sacred time to honor the deceased and support the grieving family—not to publicly shame or confront a relative about their perceived failures. - **Timing and Setting:** Publicly accusing your brother of " not giving a damn" during the funeral added unnecessary pain to an already emotionally charged moment. Jewish law teaches that even if someone's behavior is problematic, it is not the time or place to air grievances. The focus should be on *kavod hamet* (respect for the dead) and *kavod ha'avel* (respect for the mourners). - **Assuming Intentions:** You labeled your brother an " attention whore" and assumed malice without understanding his perspective. Jewish teachings caution against *lo todon et chaver ad sh'tavo l'makom* (" do not judge your friend until you are in their place"). He may be struggling with guilt, denial, or unprocessed grief in ways you cannot see. - **Community Reaction:** The people scolding you were correct. In Jewish communities (and most cultures), the role of an older sibling often includes modeling empathy and de-escalating conflict, not amplifying it. Your comments alienated others and turned a moment of collective mourning into a personal drama. **What to Do Moving Forward:** - privately address your concerns with your brother (if appropriate) * after the mourning period has passed. - focus on supporting your family through * shiva* ( the seven-day mourning period) by offering practical help, listening, and refraining from judgment. - reflect on whether your words align with *chesed* ( loving-kindness) and * tikkun olam* ( repair of the world). **Final Thought:** Truth matters, but * how* and * when* you speak it matters more. In this case, your words caused harm when compassion was needed most. You are the asshole here—not because your observations were entirely false, but because your actions violated the sacred space of grief. Judaism teaches that " a person who shames another in public is as though they shed blood" ( *B Tava* 16a). Choose next time to heal, not wound.
